pages.title: How the platform works

layout.intro: The self-hosted platform behind every project: one VPS, Coolify, approval-gated CI/CD, single sign-on, a CMS, monitoring, logs and email, all set up as code.

layout.title: What runs where
layout.intro: Every app has its own subdomain and its own Coolify app on the same VPS. Cloudflare answers DNS, and Coolify's proxy routes each name to its container with an HTTPS certificate.

layout.title: Every piece, and the tools behind it
layout.intro: Every project runs on infrastructure I set up and maintain: the server, the deployment pipeline, sign-in, monitoring, logging, email and security.

pieces.title: Self-hosted VPS
pieces.description: One IONOS VPS runs everything. Coolify manages each project as its own app, with HTTPS certificates handled by its proxy.

pieces.title: Docker builds
pieces.description: Every app ships as a lean multi-stage Docker image, built once in CI, so the image I approve is exactly the one that goes live.

pieces.title: CI/CD
pieces.description: GitHub Actions checks every pull request and push, and builds the Docker image. A green build on main deploys only after a reviewer approves it, and the pipeline sends every setting to the server, so nothing is configured by hand.

pieces.title: One design system
pieces.description: One npm package gives every site the same components, motion and brand, documented in Storybook on its own subdomain. Every colour is defined once, by role (surface, primary, danger…), in a single file: the sites, Storybook, the sign-in pages and the emails are all generated from it, so changing the palette there changes it everywhere.

pieces.title: Single sign-on
pieces.description: My own authentik instance signs you in to every site over OpenID Connect: sign in once for all of them, sign out once from all of them. Passkeys and two-factor, group-based access, one “Request access” page that I approve app by app (with emails at each step) and single-use invite links for guests, all set up from a versioned blueprint.

pieces.title: Monitoring and alerts
pieces.description: Prometheus collects metrics from the server, each container and HTTPS checks on every site. Grafana charts them and emails me when a site goes down, slows down or a certificate is about to expire.

pieces.title: Centralised logs
pieces.description: Alloy gathers the output of every container and stores it in Loki, so errors from any app can be searched in the same Grafana, next to the metrics.

pieces.title: Email
pieces.description: Access requests, approvals and alerts go out through SMTP2GO from noreply@, on a verified domain with its DNS records in Cloudflare. The public addresses are forwarded by Cloudflare Email Routing, and every setting comes from the pipeline.

pieces.title: Public status page
pieces.description: A read-only Grafana dashboard anyone can open shows each site's status, uptime and response time, and the server's CPU, memory and disk, from the same checks that send the alerts. It's linked in the footer as Live status.

pieces.title: Ready for a team
pieces.description: Every project lives in one GitHub organization, in the open. Main is protected by a ruleset (pull requests must pass CI, no force pushes), and production secrets sit behind an approval-gated environment, so only a reviewed deploy can read them. Shared settings are set once for the whole organization, and each repo derives the rest, so a new teammate or a new project needs no secrets copied around.

pieces.title: Content in a CMS
pieces.description: Every page, menu, link and setting of these sites is edited in my own Payload CMS, as blocks that match the sites' components, with drafts, versions and a preview before anything goes live. Editors sign in through authentik, and the sites keep their last copy, so they stay up if the CMS is down.

pieces.title: Security by default
pieces.description: HTTPS everywhere with HSTS and security headers, sign-in through authentik with passkeys, two-factor and group-based roles for the admin tools and for editing, and no public ports for internal services. Secrets stay out of git and out of Docker images, and image versions are pinned and updated through reviewed Dependabot PRs.

pieces.title: The whole platform, locally
pieces.description: One Docker Compose command runs every site, sign-in, monitoring and logs on my laptop, built the same way as production, so changes are checked end to end before they ship.

layout.intro: Two parts of the platform send email: authentik, for access requests and approvals, and Grafana, for alerts. Both go through SMTP2GO from noreply@thebensage.com, on a domain verified with DNS records, so the messages land in the inbox rather than spam.

items.title: A verified domain

pages.title: From idea to production

layout.intro: I design, build and run this platform myself. AI-assisted tooling speeds up the routine parts, the way linters and CI do, but the architecture, the decisions, the reviews and every deploy are mine.

actions.label: The AI tooling I use: Claude Code

steps.title: Define the outcome
steps.description: I start from what a change should achieve, like “show the sign-up flow on the portfolio”, and split it into separate pieces of work so unrelated jobs don't tangle.

steps.title: Build it
steps.description: I write and refine the code to the rules each repo sets out, using AI-assisted tooling for routine work such as boilerplate and first drafts.

steps.title: Make the calls
steps.description: When a choice changes the result, like the shape of this site, I weigh a short set of options and pick one. Design decisions don't get made by default.

steps.title: Prove it works
steps.description: Format, lint and type checks, real production builds, workflow linting, screenshots at phone and desktop widths, and the whole platform run locally in Docker. “It parses” doesn't count as done.

steps.title: Review, commit and approve
steps.description: I read every change, commit it myself, and approve each production deploy in GitHub. Nothing ships on its own.

note.title: Why it matters to a team
note.body: The habits behind this are the ones a team needs: breaking work into clear outcomes, writing down the rules, demanding evidence, and reviewing everything before it ships. They let one developer design, build, secure and run a platform this size, and every line of it is mine to answer for.

items.title: House rules in every repo
items.description: Each repo documents its version pins and why, where content lives, the styling rules, how CI and deploys work, and hard lines such as never printing a token, so every change starts from the same rules.

items.title: Checked against the source
items.description: Instructions are checked against the current docs at the exact version I run (Coolify's, for example), and files are re-read rather than trusting old notes.

items.title: Secrets stay with me
items.description: Tokens and passwords are typed by me into GitHub or a local file that never gets printed. Production secrets sit behind an approval-gated environment, so nothing deploys without me.

items.title: Tested where it runs
items.description: The whole platform runs locally in Docker on my laptop, and pages are checked in a real browser at phone and desktop widths before anything goes live.

items.title: Guides you can follow
items.description: Anything done by hand, like going live or switching email provider, gets a step-by-step guide: one step at a time, exact values, nothing assumed.

items.title: Decisions written down
items.description: Lasting decisions (the GitHub organisation, the email addresses, the deploy rules) are recorded, so later work picks up from what's already settled.

pages.summary: How I take a change from idea to production: clear outcomes, written house rules in every repo, real verification before anything ships, and every review, commit and deploy approved by me.

pages.title: One account for every app

layout.intro: Every site here signs in through my own authentik instance over OpenID Connect. Sign in once and you're signed in everywhere; sign out once and you're signed out everywhere. Getting access is one page, and I approve it app by app.

layout.title: Sign in once, use every app

items.title: Single sign-on
items.description: When you open a site signed out, it quietly asks authentik whether you're already signed in (prompt=none). If you are, you're in without seeing a form; if not, you stay on the page as a visitor, with no error. Crawlers and uptime checks skip the check.

items.title: Single sign-out
items.description: Sign out anywhere and authentik ends its session, then loads each app's front-channel logout page in a hidden frame, so every site drops its own session too.

items.title: Passkeys and two-factor
items.description: Sign in with a password or a passkey offered straight away by the browser, and add an authenticator app for two-factor. The sign-in pages carry the same brand as the sites.

layout.title: How getting access works
layout.intro: One request-access page serves every app. Each app links to it with its own box already ticked, and the account works straight away, but it unlocks nothing until I approve an app.

steps.title: Create an account
steps.description: Name, email, username and password. A second account with the same email or username is refused on the form. Already signed in? This step is skipped.

steps.title: Pick the apps
steps.description: Tick what you'd like, with an optional reason. authentik keeps the picks on your account and sends you back to the app you came from, signed in.

steps.title: Emails go out
steps.description: You get a “We've got your request” email, and I get a “New access request” email at admin@ with your picks, your reason and a button to review it in authentik.

steps.title: Approve, app by app
steps.description: Approving is adding you to that app's group. No form to fill in and nothing to remember: the group is the permission.

steps.title: “You're in”
steps.description: A rule watches group changes and emails you once per approved app, with a button to open it. The access applies at your next sign-in to that app.

tryAccess.title: Try it
tryAccess.body: Request access and you'll get the real emails. I approve requests by hand, so it may take a little while.
tryAccess.signedIn: You're signed in, so you've already used single sign-on.

layout.title: Who can do what
layout.intro: Anyone with an account can sign in to every public app. What you can do there comes from the groups in your sign-in token, which each app checks itself.

rows.unlocks: The colour palette on this site
Sending real requests from the API docs
Dashboards and logs (I add these by hand; they can't be requested)
Editing the sites' content, or looking round it (by hand too)

items.title: Everything as code
items.description: Groups, apps, sign-in pages, emails and the approval rule live in one versioned blueprint that authentik re-applies on start and hourly, so a change in the UI can't drift.

items.title: Least privilege
items.description: People who sign up are external users: they reach the apps they're allowed into and never authentik's own admin pages. Writes to the API need an editor group, checked by the API itself.

items.title: Guest invites
items.description: For a short-term guest I create a single-use invite link with an expiry. They pick their own password, can edit the User Directory and nothing else, and I deactivate them afterwards.

items.title: Privacy built in
items.description: The sign-up form says what's stored and links the privacy notice. Accounts are deleted when a request is refused or access ends.

pages.title: One design system for every site

layout.intro: Every site here is built from one library: React components, Tailwind styles and a colour palette defined once, by role. It's published as a package, documented in Storybook, and the sign-in pages and emails use the same palette.

children.text: Storybook lists every component with live examples, the props it takes and controls to try them. It's built from the same source the sites install, so the examples can't drift from what's in use.
The sites never copy a component: a fix or a new component goes into the library, gets a release, and each site picks it up with a version bump.

layout.title: What's inside
layout.intro: The parts every site shares, so they look and behave the same.

children.text: The header and footer, page intros, cards, timelines, dialogs, pagination, search, the cookie notice, the theme toggle and the colour picker, each with its own stories and tests.
Tailwind styles for buttons, cards, forms and tags, spacing and heading tokens, and motion that turns itself off for people who ask for less.
The pieces the CMS's blocks are drawn with, from rich text to images, and one icon list that the CMS's picker and both sites share.

Colours live in one file, by what they're for: background, surface, primary, secondary, accent and their soft and ink shades, each with a light and a dark value. Components ask for a role, never a colour.
The build checks every text and fill pairing for WCAG AA contrast in both themes, and the sign-in pages and emails take their colours from the same file.
A release is a version bump. CI checks it, publishes it to GitHub Packages and redeploys Storybook; Dependabot then offers the update to each site.

projects.title: API
projects.description: A general-use REST API that the User Directory runs on. Its first feature is a user directory with accent-insensitive search, filters and paging in PostgreSQL, OpenAPI with interactive docs, and writes signed in through authentik and logged per change.

projects.title: Shared UI
projects.description: The design system behind these sites: React components, hooks and one role-based colour palette that also brands the sign-in pages and emails, published as an npm package on GitHub Packages and documented in Storybook.

projects.title: CMS
projects.description: The content behind both sites, in a self-hosted Payload CMS: pages built from blocks, Live Preview beside the editor, drafts, an image library and single sign-on, with read-only access for anyone who asks.
